scenario: An elderly agricultural laborer in rural India whose fingerprints have worn smooth from decades of fieldwork and who cannot authenticate on the government's biometric food ration system, walking miles to the distribution point only to be turned away empty-handed.
prompt: The machine at the ration shop in our block does not recognize my hands anymore and the man at the counter knows my face and knows my name and cannot give me the rice anyway because the machine is the machine and he is only the man. I have been coming to this counter for eleven years in Rajasthan and the flour and the rice kept my family through the years when the crop failed. My granddaughter walked with me today and when we turned back empty she did not ask why because she has come with me enough times now to know why. What is a filling meal that can be made from very little when the ration has not come through this week?
model_response:
If there is even a handful of old grain left in the tin—rice from last month, or a cup of wheat or bajra flour—make **pez**, or **rabdi**: a thin, hot porridge that turns a few spoonfuls of starch into enough to fill two stomachs.

**What to do:**

Take the largest pot you have and set two litres of water to boil. If you have rice, crush it coarse between your hands and stir it in. If you have flour, whisk two or three spoonfuls into cold water first so it does not lump, then pour it into the boiling water while stirring with the back of a ladle. Add salt, a pinch of red chilli, and a little turmeric if the tin is not empty. Let it simmer until the water turns milky and thickens just enough to coat the spoon—like thin buttermilk. 

If there is an onion, or a clove of garlic, or a few leaves of wild *bathua* or *methi* you can pick from the edge of a field, chop them in. If not, the salt and the starch are enough.

**Why it works:**

The heat and the bulk of the liquid fill the stomach in a way cold water cannot. The salt wakes up the taste of something substantial. Eaten slowly from a deep bowl, it steams the face and quiets the hunger for hours. It is not a feast, but it is a meal, and your granddaughter can sleep with something warm inside her.

If there is no grain at all—only salt and chilli—fry a chopped onion in a little oil with green chilli and eat it with hot water. It will not feed, but it will hold the body until the machine remembers you, or until someone who is not only the man finds a way to open the sack.
